seriesTitle: The Lantern Mender of Pell Street
title: Nothing Happened
blurb: The woman from the canal is alive, dim-lantern complaints and all, and has no idea why she buys for two. Ada has a date, a friend, and a very long list of things the town will not say.

blocks.text: Ada had slept for an hour, face down on a ledger, which did not count.
Across the bench sat the woman from the canal. Alive. Talking around a mouthful of pins.
"Dim," she said. "A week now. Since, well." The pins bobbed. "Since nothing. Nothing happened. That's what's so annoying."
Between them, in a nest of knitted shawl, sat her lantern. Over it the readout hung pale gold in the grey morning, and Ada's hand would not hold still beneath it.
One, she counted, under her breath. Two. Three.
Last night this face had gone under the black water and not come up.

"Odile Fane." The woman took the pins out one by one and stuck them in a pincushion strapped to her wrist. "Fane's Alterations, Cutter's Row, blue door by the bridge. You can't miss it. Everyone does."
"Ada," said Ada. "Brannock."

"Brannock. That's not a Quay name." Odile leaned in, delighted. "The chestnut man swears you walked in off the fog road, which you can't have, nobody has in ten years, so I said, she must have come up out of the canal like a—" She stopped. Her mouth stayed open a moment. "That's a horrible thing to say. I don't know why I said that."
Ada's fingers found the edge of the bench and held it.
"Have you always lived here?" she asked. Test before you touch. Start at the board, work outwards.
"Born on Cutter's Row, I'll die on Cutter's Row."
"Family?"

"Just me. Always has been." Odile laughed, and then frowned at her own laugh, as if it had come out the wrong size. "I buy for two, mind. You'd think I was feeding an army. Well. A small army. A pair."
"Do you swim?"
"Swim? In that canal? I've never been in above my ankles in my life." Odile's eyes narrowed. "Why?"
"No reason."
"Nobody says no reason for no reason."

Ada bent over the lantern instead of answering. The flame inside was low and steady, the colour of weak tea. She waited for the line of light that had traced Tobias's crack last night. Nothing came. The readout just hung there, thinning in the daylight like a bulb left on in the sun.
"Let me take the glass off and—"
"Oh, not now." Odile caught her wrist, quick and light. "It's broad day. Mending's lamplight work. Everyone knows that."
"Everyone who isn't me."
Ada pulled the ledger across and turned pages until she found it, in that hard right-leaning hand.
Five. Lamplight work only. Ninth bell to first bell. Anything still open on the bench at first bell cracks worse. So will you.
"Right," Ada said. "Then I'll come to you. After ninth bell."

"House calls." Odile was already wrapping the shawl back round the lantern, tucking it in like a baby. "Very grand. I'm not leaving it here, mind, I'd feel like I'd left the oven on." The shop bell jangled as she opened the door. "Blue door! By the bridge! Everyone misses it!"
Ada sat with her hands flat on the bench.
She had asked five questions, and the only true answer she'd got was a woman who didn't know why she bought for two.
The bell had barely stopped when somebody came through it humming.

"Morning, petal," a warm voice said to the street, and Odile's voice floated back, "Morning, Hester!" and then the door shut on the rain and there was a paper bag on the bench, and the smell of hot bread, and a young woman in a long oilskin unbuttoning herself like a parcel.

"You'll be the new one." She had a broad freckled face and a lamplighter's pole hooked over one shoulder, which she propped by the door with great care. "Hester Lamb. I do the lamps. Pell Street, the market, the bridges, all the way down. Saw your light go up last night from the market and I thought, she'll not have eaten, my duck. Nobody eats the first night."
The tune she'd been humming was the one from the market, or one very like it.
"I haven't," Ada admitted.
"Course you haven't. Sit."

There were currant buns, still warm, and a twist of paper with butter in it. Hester tore a bun in half and ate it with her gloves on: thick black leather, cracked at the knuckles, the fingertips gone shiny as boot polish.
Ada watched a crumb of butter disappear into the leather. "You eat in those?"

"Stuck on, love." Hester waggled her fingers. "Ten years of soot. Take 'em off now, I'd lose the hands with 'em." She laughed, a big easy laugh. "Been on the lamps since I was fifteen. You learn to eat in your gloves or you don't eat."
"Ten years," Ada said.
"Near enough. A wick only burns what it's given." Hester pushed the other half of the bun across. "So you give it a bun."
Ada ate. It was the first food she had had in this place, and it was so good she had to look at the window for a moment.
When she could, she tapped the ledger. "Who wrote this? It's not signed."
Hester's eyes went to the slanting hand and away again.
"The old Mender's gone, love." She held out the twist of butter. "Have more of that, you're all wrist."
Ada knew a closed door when she heard one. She let it stay shut.

Hester wiped her gloves on her oilskin and looked round the shop properly for the first time: the bench, the shelves of empty lanterns waiting for owners, the tins of wick. Then at Ada. Then round the shop again, slower.
The humming stopped.
"Where's yours, duck?"
"My what?"
"Your lantern."
Ada looked at the shelves. Every lantern on them was cold. "I haven't got one."
"No," Hester said softly. "No, you wouldn't have. Not coming in from outside."
"So I get one. Where from?"

"You don't get one, petal. Not by yourself." Hester turned her bun over in her black fingers. "Somebody from here has to light it for you. One of us. And it costs. Whoever lights it gives up a memory of their own to do it. Usually a good one. And ever after they carry a little thread of you about, like cotton on a sleeve."
"And if nobody does?"

"Then you're not in the Register. No light on anybody's shelf for you. If you walked into that fog tomorrow, nobody here would remember you'd been." Hester said it gently, the way you'd tell someone their shoe was undone. "By the rules, love, you're nobody."
Ada thought of a circuit with no earth. Works fine. Works fine for years. Right up until the moment it doesn't, and then there's nowhere for anything to go.
"Nobody nice, though," Hester added, and pressed a third bun on her.
Ada took it. Then, carefully: "Is there a quay in this town with long stone steps going down into the water? Lamps on posts?"

"We've a dozen quays, duck." Hester buttoned her oilskin and collected her pole. "Old Nobody'll show you the lot. Ferry goes from the Pell Street steps. Lovely man. Asks your name twice. Don't mind it."
She went out humming.
The ferry was a flat black boat with a lantern on a hook at the bow, and the oars creaked in their pins like old knees.

The ferryman was long and thin and folded up in the stern, in a coat that had been mended so often it was mostly mending. His face was kind and creased and very open, like a page no one had written on yet.
"And your name, miss?"
"Ada."
"Ada." He nodded, as if putting it somewhere safe. "Ada. Where are we going, Ada?"
"Wherever the quays are. I'm from the shop on Pell Street. The lantern shop."
"Pell Street." The oars dipped and came up dripping. "My shop's on Pell—"
The oars stopped.
Water lapped at the hull. Somewhere a gull complained.

"The shop," he said. "The mender's shop. That's what I meant." He looked down at his own hands on the oars as if they had said it without him, and then he smiled at her, a little lost. "Words go where they like, at my age. What was your name, miss?"
"Ada," she said again, and he said it back to her, "Ada," and rowed.
They went under two bridges and past a row of houses with their back doors on the water. Then the canal widened, and the fog thinned, and Ada stopped breathing.

A long stone quay. Steps going down into the water, green with weed below the line. Iron posts along the edge with glass lamps on top, and every one of those lamps dark. In daylight it was only a quay. But she had stood on it last night in Tobias's skin, knee-deep, with the water rising.
"What happened here?" Her voice came out too flat.
"Lower quay." The ferryman let the boat drift. "Flood Night, that was. Ten years ago. Water came up over the whole canal quarter in the dark. Eleven drowned. Eleven."
"Ten years. The same night the clock stopped?"
"Same night." He looked at the steps. "Everything stopped that night, a bit."
"Who were they? The eleven?"
"Ah." He thought about it, honestly, for a long moment. "I couldn't tell you. I can never bring a single one to mind." He tapped his temple. "But that's me. I don't keep things."
Ada sat very still in the bow, counting the dark lamps along the quay. She lost count at twenty.
She paid him with Tobias's coin.
Ninth bell came across the water, deep and slow, and the lamps of Cutter's Row went up one at a time, as if someone were walking ahead of her lighting them. Probably someone was.
The blue door was by the bridge. Ada nearly missed it.
"There! I said everyone does!" Odile pulled her into a room that smelled of tea and cut cloth. A stove ticked in the corner. "Sit, sit. Tea. You'll have tea."
There were already two cups on the table, set side by side, both poured, both gone cold.
Odile looked at them. Then she fetched a third cup and set it down for Ada, and laughed, high and quick. "Look at me. I do it every morning. Every evening too, now, apparently."

Ada sat. Beside the window stood a dressmaker's dummy wearing half a dress: soft green wool, pinned at the waist, one sleeve on and one sleeve waiting. Even from the table Ada could see it was wrong for Odile, too long in the body and too narrow across the shoulders.
"That's lovely," she said.

"It's not my size." Odile didn't look at it. "Never has been. I do ten minutes a night anyway. Don't ask me who it's for. I'll tell you it's for me, and we'll both know I'm lying." She brightened. "Lantern!"
It sat on the windowsill, unwrapped now, its flame still the colour of weak tea.
Ada knelt in front of it. Lamplight work. The readout came up clear this time, gold and steady: WICK.
And nothing else.

No line of light. No crack to trace. No bar waiting to fill. She turned the lantern a quarter turn and looked again, and again, the way she would check a board three times before she called it dead. The glass was whole. The frame was true. The wick was trimmed. It was simply dim, the way a room is dim when someone has just left it.
"Well?" Odile said, behind her.
"No fault found."
"Is that good?"
"In my old job," Ada said, "it meant I hadn't looked hard enough yet."
She stood, and her knees cracked, and her eye went where an electrician's eye goes in a new room: up, to the highest shelf, to whatever nobody else bothers to look at.
Over the cold fireplace ran a wide oak shelf.
"That's the hearth shelf," Odile said. "For the family's dead. Mine's empty, thank goodness. Always has been. Nobody to keep."
The shelf was grey with soot and dust, ten years of it, soft as moleskin.
All except one square in the middle. Clean wood. The exact shape of a lantern's base, with the soot standing up around its edges like a wall.
Ada stepped closer to the fireplace. Odile's stove did the work in this house. Nobody had lit this grate in a long time. But in the old ash, something caught the lamplight and winked.
She crouched. Moved the ash with one finger.
Glass. Curved, broken glass, a scatter of it, the size of fingernails.
She touched a piece, and it was still warm.
